title: Injecting Services Into Views and Action Methods
description: Use @inject in Razor views and [FromServices] on action methods to consume DI services exactly where they are needed.

terms.definition: A Razor directive that resolves a service from the DI container and makes it available as a property in the view.
An MVC attribute placed on an action method parameter that causes the DI container to resolve it instead of the model binder.
The raw key-value configuration API; useful for one-off lookups but less type-safe than the options pattern.
Strongly typed configuration injected into a Razor view via @inject IOptions<T>.

data.text: Constructor injection is the standard approach, but it isn't always the right fit. Sometimes only one action method needs a service, or a Razor view needs data the controller didn't pass. ASP.NET Core provides two narrower alternatives: `[FromServices]` for action methods and `@inject` for views.
Add `[FromServices]` to an action parameter when only that method needs the service. The container resolves it at call time, keeping the controller constructor lean.

data.content: Resolving ProductSummary only for the Summary action method

data.title: When to use [FromServices]
data.text: Use [FromServices] when one or two actions need a service but most don't. If most actions need it, use constructor injection to keep the dependency contract explicit.
The `@inject` directive resolves a service directly inside a Razor view. It is most useful for reading configuration in layout pages or rendering small pieces of data without controller involvement.

data.text: Passing Data From Controller to View (Preferred)
A cleaner alternative to `@inject` is to resolve the service in the controller and pass the result via the model or ViewBag. This keeps the view free of DI concerns and is far easier to unit test.

data.text: For quick, one-off key lookups, inject `IConfiguration` directly. This is less type-safe than the options pattern but useful for ad-hoc reads.

data.title: Rules of thumb
items: Use constructor injection by default — it makes all dependencies explicit.
Use [FromServices] when only one or two actions need a service.
Use @inject only for layout-level or read-only configuration concerns.
Never resolve services manually with new inside controllers or views.
Prefer IOptions<T> over raw IConfiguration lookups in all production code.

data.title: Exercise: Apply the Right Injection Technique
data.description: Given a controller and layout view, choose and apply the correct DI technique for each scenario.
steps: A WeatherController needs ApiSettings for every action — inject via constructor.
A single ExportPdf action needs IReportGenerator only for that action — use [FromServices].
A _Layout.cshtml needs the app name from IOptions<AppSettings> — use @inject.
A product list is rendered from the controller's model — keep the view free of @inject.
data.expectedOutcome: A controller with constructor-injected shared services, [FromServices] on one-off actions, and @inject used only in the layout where the controller cannot pass the data.

items.question: Is [FromServices] the same as constructor injection?
items.answer: The service comes from the same DI container either way. The difference is scope: [FromServices] resolves per action call, while constructor injection resolves once per controller instance.

items.question: Can I @inject a Scoped service into a view?
items.answer: Yes. Views run within the HTTP request scope, so Scoped services are available. The same lifetime rules apply — do not use Scoped services inside Singletons.

items.question: Should I inject into views or pass data from the controller?
items.answer: Passing from the controller is preferred. It keeps views simpler and makes controllers unit-testable. Use @inject for layout-level or read-only configuration concerns.

items.question: Can I use @inject inside a partial view?
items.answer: Yes. @inject works in any Razor file: views, partials, layouts, and view components. Each file resolves its own injection independently.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Constructor injection is the default — it makes all dependencies explicit and testable.
[FromServices] is the right choice when only one action needs a service.
@inject is useful in layout pages and for read-only configuration, but prefer passing data from the controller.
IOptions<T> gives typed, IntelliSense-supported access to configuration everywhere.
Choose the narrowest injection point that fits — it keeps code clean, testable, and loosely coupled.
data.takeaway: ASP.NET Core gives you many injection points. Use constructor injection by default, and reach for [FromServices] or @inject only when you have a specific reason to narrow the scope.
